extracted.intended_audience: referees/reviewers for Theoretical Economics (economists, including early-career referees)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing referee reports for submissions to Theoretical Economics, aimed at helping referees (especially junior economists) produce useful, professional, and actionable reviews that enable editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest check before accepting
rubrics_metrics.description: Before accepting to referee a paper, a referee should ensure that they do not have a conflict of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees must verify the absence of conflicts before agreeing to review; consult the Society's code of conduct for guidance (especially for members).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult the Econometric Society code of conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The econometric society's code of conduct is also an important reference for referees (especially for those who are members of the econometric society).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the code of conduct as a touchstone for appropriate behavior, confidentiality, and conflict rules while reviewing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose: help the Editor make a decision
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary purpose of the report is to help the Editor make a decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the report to give the Editor a clear interpretation of the paper and a basis for accept/reject/revise decisions. If recommending revision, provide sufficient and specific conditions for publication; avoid asking for additions that would only be lateral or speculative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide explicit recommendation and appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: The report should include a clear appraisal and an explicit recommendation. The bottom line recommendation may be in the report or in the cover letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State accept/reject/revise (or other verdict) clearly. Use the cover letter if you need to explain nuances. If recommending revise & resubmit, explain precisely what is necessary for you to support publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable revision requests (R&R as a contract)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are recommending a revise & resubmit (or you are on the fence), you should explain what is necessary to meet the bar. The revise & resubmit should be thought of as a contract: if the author meets your requests, then you will recommend the paper be published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be as precise and explicit as possible about required changes. Keep revision requests reasonable and avoid speculative or open-ended demands; at TE editors aim to make up/down decisions on the second round.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject when author cannot meet requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is no way the author can satisfy your requirements, the paper should be rejected, no matter how much you like it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rejection rather than offering R&R when the paper's deficiencies are such that necessary changes are infeasible; when rejecting, be explicit about reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polite, professional, and honest tone
rubrics_metrics.description: It is very important that your report be polite and professional, while providing an honest assessment. Treat others like you would like to be treated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain civility even when critical. Clear, respectful language increases the usefulness of the report and reduces antagonism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a concise summary of the paper
rubrics_metrics.description: A referee report typically summarizes the paper in a couple of paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize how you interpret the paper to put later comments in context. The summary also signals whether the paper's content is effectively conveyed (if unclear, you may have missed a key element).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion: explain strengths, weaknesses, and use length as criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: This section should explain the strengths and weaknesses of the paper. Length should be used as a criterion in the assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss substantive merits and flaws; consider whether the paper is too long or unfocused and whether length affects clarity or contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit when recommending rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If you recommend that the paper be rejected, you should strive to be as explicit as possible in the reasons for rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear, concrete reasons so the Editor and authors understand the decision basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive comments: distinguish necessary vs desirable
rubrics_metrics.description: This section should elaborate on the above opinion. Try to be as clear as possible about which issues are necessary for the revision, and which are desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number and structure substantive points so authors can address them; separate essential fixes from optional improvements; avoid suggesting extensions that are not essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbered, structured comments
rubrics_metrics.description: These comments should be numbered so the author can refer to them in any revision. They should also be structured, so each comment gets a separate number, rather than having comments flow into other comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numbered lists and distinct items for clarity. Each numbered comment should present a single issue or request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid requesting non-essential extensions and extra appendices
rubrics_metrics.description: The report should suggest only extensions that are essential for the paper at hand. Any additional request can lead the paper to become bloated, and waste the author’s time. In particular, suggestions to add material in the form of extra appendices (especially supplementary online ones) should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ask for peripheral robustness checks or sprawling extensions; TE generally discourages supplementary appendices that expand length without improving the core paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: State how the paper can be made shorter and more focused
rubrics_metrics.description: You should state if (and how) the paper can be made shorter. Which results should be prioritized, and which should be cut? Can the paper be made more succinct, and the proofs shorter, if the results are less general?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give concrete guidance on pruning or prioritizing results and shortening proofs; indicate tradeoffs between generality and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smaller/presentational comments separated from substantive ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller/Presentational comments: These are best separated from the more substantial comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place presentational issues (typos, formatting, minor clarity fixes) in a separate section. You need not point out every typo but should highlight systematic problem areas. Avoid recommending material be moved to supplementary appendices that disguise true length; TE generally discourages such appendices.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI use policy for referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees reviewing a manuscript for the journals of the Society are expected to read the submission themselves and form their own independent evaluation of the work. Referees may use AI tools to help shape and communicate their views—for example, to improve the clarity of suggestions, to organize comments, or to polish the language of the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any use of AI must not replace the referee's independent judgment; the report must reflect the referee’s own evaluation. Use AI only as an assistive tool (editing, organizing, clarifying).
